title: Historical Date Converter
plainSentence: A converter that lets you turn a past date into the calendar another country used then, and warns when that date never existed.
pitch: Pick a date between 1500 and 1930 and a place, and the page shows what that day was called under the old Julian calendar and the modern Gregorian one, with the weekday, the day count and a clear flag when the date was skipped there. It opens on today's date in 1582, a day that did not exist in Rome, so the first result is a surprise. Genealogists, history writers and curious people get a private, offline answer with the working shown step by step.
firstMinute: The page opens with 13 October 1582 in Rome already entered and the result on screen: that date never existed there, the calendar jumped from Thursday 4 October to Friday 15 October, and the same day in England was 3 October. One button swaps in any other date or place, so the visitor gets a first success without reading anything.
conceptsToLearn: A calendar date can name different days depending on which calendar a country was using at the time.
whyNow: Today is 13 October, a date inside the ten days (5 to 14 October 1582) that were skipped in Rome, Spain and Portugal. The topic is timeless for anyone reading old letters, parish records or diaries.

purposeDetail.job: Convert a historical date between the Julian and Gregorian calendars using the switch date of the chosen country, and say when the date was skipped or ambiguous.
purposeDetail.audience: Family-history researchers, history students, writers and anyone reading old documents, letters or diaries dated before their country changed calendars.
purposeDetail.freeGap: Free general Julian-to-Gregorian converters exist, and a genealogy magazine points to old-style/new-style converters. No paywall claim is verified, so none is made. The remaining gap: one page that is private and offline, knows each region's own switch date, flags skipped dates and the old 25 March New Year, and shows every step of the arithmetic.
purposeDetail.oracle: Julian Day Number relations documented in the Julian day reference and in the IDL JULDAY documentation (4 and 15 October 1582 are consecutive days in the day count), the Gregorian leap rule, and the published skips: Rome 4 to 15 October 1582, Britain 2 to 14 September 1752.
purposeDetail.inputs: A year, month and day, plus a region from a bundled list of about 20 places with their switch dates, and an optional choice of which calendar the date was written in.
purposeDetail.outputs: The date in both calendars, the weekday, the Julian Day Number, a dual-date form such as 1731/32 for dates before the New Year moved, a skipped-date warning, and days between two dates across a switch. Results can be copied as text.
purposeDetail.limits: Switch dates varied inside some countries (German states, Swiss cantons, colonies); the page uses one date per region and says so. It does not handle non-Christian calendars, and it is not legal or genealogical proof.

research.summary: In Rome, Spain, Portugal and most of Italy the day after Thursday 4 October 1582 was Friday 15 October, so 5 to 14 October 1582 never happened there, and today's date (13 October) is one of them. Britain and its colonies skipped 2 to 14 September 1752. Day counts such as the Julian Day Number run on without a gap, which gives a clean oracle. The famous riots over lost days in 1752 are largely a myth, which suits a corrections box. Switch dates elsewhere (Russia 1918, Greece 1923, Sweden 1753) came back only from blended or single results and stay unverified for now.

facts.claim: In Rome, Spain, Portugal and most of Italy, Thursday 4 October 1582 was followed by Friday 15 October 1582, so 5 to 14 October 1582 do not exist there.
Britain and its colonies moved to the Gregorian calendar so that Wednesday 2 September 1752 was followed by Thursday 14 September 1752, and New Year's Day moved from 25 March to 1 January.

Oracle: the day count is continuous across the 1582 switch; 4 October 1582 (Julian) and 15 October 1582 (Gregorian) are consecutive days, with Julian day numbers 2299160 and 2299161 in the IDL documentation example.

The Gregorian rule makes a year a leap year if divisible by 4, except century years not divisible by 400, giving 97 leap years per 400 years and an average year of 365.2425 days; the Julian average of 365.25 days gains about 3.1 days per 400 years.
Historians treat the story of 1752 mobs demanding their eleven days back as largely a myth; the slogan is tied to a 1755 painting and a 1754 election, with some smaller real protests.
As reported in a blended search summary, as of 2026-10-13: Russia moved from 31 January to 14 February 1918 and Greece adopted Gregorian civil dates in 1923. Not confirmed by two separate results.

As reported by timeanddate and an SBS feature (seen in a blended summary), Sweden skipped 11 days in February 1753 after the 1712 extra 30 February. Not confirmed; the page would say 'per timeanddate' or leave Sweden out.
As reported by Family Tree Magazine, researchers should check each country's switch date and may meet dual years such as 1747OS and 1748NS. Single source.

A built-in known-answer table is visible on the page.

A self-test panel that re-runs the published known answers in the visitor's browser

title: Equation of Time Lesson
plainSentence: A lesson that lets you slide through the year to see why a sundial runs minutes ahead of or behind your clock.
pitch: Start on today's date with a sundial and a clock side by side, then drag through the year and watch the gap rise and fall. Three short demos separate the two causes (a tilted axis and an oval orbit), explain why the earliest sunset comes weeks before the shortest day, and show how railways and a 13 October 1884 vote replaced every town's own sun time. Check-yourself questions end each step.
firstMinute: The page opens on 13 October with a sundial reading and a clock reading shown together and the gap printed in minutes. Dragging the year slider moves both and draws the gap curve, so the visitor sees the sun run ahead of and behind the clock before reading a word.
whyNow: On 13 October 1884 delegates at the International Meridian Conference voted for Greenwich as the world's zero line, the step that ended each town keeping its own sun time. In mid-October the sundial also runs several minutes ahead of the clock, and the earliest sunsets of winter are weeks away.

purposeDetail.concept: The equation of time: why solar time (what a sundial shows) and clock time (mean solar time) differ by up to about a quarter of an hour during the year, and how longitude and time zones add a second, separate offset.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Most people learn that noon is when the sun is highest and the day is longest on the solstice. The idea that sunrise, noon and sunset drift against the clock all year is rarely taught, yet it explains everyday puzzles like the earliest sunset coming before the shortest day.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious adults and older students, hobby astronomers, sundial and photography fans, anyone who has wondered why sunset times keep changing after the solstice.
misconceptions: The earliest sunset of the year falls on the shortest day (winter solstice).
Solar noon is always at 12:00 clock time at the middle of a time zone.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Sunrise and sunset sit on either side of solar noon, and solar noon itself drifts against the clock; so in early December the sun sets earlier even as the day's length is still falling more slowly, and the earliest sunset arrives weeks before the solstice.
demos: Sundial and clock side by side with a day-of-year slider and a live gap curve, opening on today's date.
Two-cause split: switch on only the tilted axis, only the oval orbit, then both, and watch the two small curves add into the real one.
Longitude ladder: pick a town, see the 4-minutes-per-degree offset from its zone's central line, and replay the 18 November 1883 railway switch with the 'two noons' effect.
Sunset finder: choose a latitude and find the earliest sunset and the shortest day, then see the gap between them.
checkQuestions: On 3 November is a sundial ahead of or behind the clock, and by about how much?
If a town is 2 degrees of longitude west of its zone's central line, how many minutes later does its sun reach the highest point?
Why does the earliest sunset not fall on the winter solstice in the northern hemisphere?
Which single cause gives a half-year rhythm and which gives a one-year rhythm?

research.summary: Delegates at the 1884 International Meridian Conference voted on 13 October for Greenwich (22 for, 1 against, 2 abstaining), a few months after North American railways replaced local sun times on 18 November 1883. Local time changes by 4 minutes per degree of longitude. The puzzle that the earliest sunset comes before the shortest day is documented by several independent outlets and traces to the equation of time. Exact extremes of the equation of time (about +16 min 33 s in early November and -14 min 6 s in mid February) and the split between tilt and orbit shape were seen only in blended summaries, so the page will compute them and label them as computed, not as quoted.

facts.claim: On 13 October 1884 the International Meridian Conference voted to adopt the Greenwich meridian: 22 for, 1 against, with France and Brazil abstaining; the formal resolutions were adopted on 22 October.
On 18 November 1883 North American railroads moved from many local sun times to zone standard time, known as the Day of Two Noons; New York's timekeeper paused the clock for 3 minutes 58 seconds.
Local mean time shifts by 4 minutes per degree of longitude, while standard time steps by one hour per 15 degrees.

In the northern hemisphere the earliest sunset of the year comes before the winter solstice (for New York 7 to 8 December in the 2025 table) because solar noon drifts later on the clock; the shortest day and the earliest sunset are different events.

As reported, unconfirmed: the equation of time peaks near +16 min 33 s around 3 November and dips to about -14 min 6 s around 11 February, driven by the tilt of the axis (about 23.44 degrees, the larger part) and the orbit's eccentricity (about 0.0167). The page computes these values and labels them computed.

design.coreLoop: Demo, question, aha: drag the year to see the gap, answer a prediction question before revealing the next demo, split the gap into its two causes, then use the sunset finder to confirm the earliest-sunset surprise; each step ends with a check question and a plain-language summary.

Longitude ladder with a replay of the 1883 railway switch
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: four demos, an intro paragraph, glossary, check questions, a small bundled list of about 40 cities with longitudes. Cut: full analemma 3-D view, daylight-saving rules, high-latitude polar day edge cases, live fetching.
risks: The equation-of-time extremes and the tilt-versus-orbit split are unverified in this dossier (blended summary); the verifier should read the sundial-society document or another source, or the page shows computed values labelled 'computed here'.
Oracle for the computed curve is not yet pinned to a published vector; builders should compare against the extremes above and a published almanac or solar-calculator table, naming it on the page.
Sunset timing needs a careful sunrise-equation implementation; refraction and elevation are ignored and the page says 'about a minute'.
Delegate counts for the 1884 conference differ between sources (25, 26 or 27 nations); the page quotes only the vote date and 22-1 tally.

title: Poker Chips Aren't Dollars
plainSentence: A lesson that shows, with sliders and exact sums, why a tournament player's chips are worth less than their share of the prize money.
pitch: Poker tournament threads keep asking the same thing: why would anyone fold a big hand near the money? This lesson answers it with a ladder of live demos: set the stacks and prizes, watch chip share and prize-money share drift apart, then test a bubble all-in and see the exact extra winning chance a call needs. Every number is computed in the page and the sum is shown step by step, with simulated chips only.
firstMinute: The first frame already shows three stacks and a 50/30/20 prize split, with a bar for each player's chip share beside a bar for the prize money the model gives them (the 50% stack gets about 38%). Sliding any stack makes both bars move at once, so the gap is seen before any text is read. A one-line caption names the gap, and that is the first success.
conceptsToLearn: A tournament pays prizes by finishing place, not by how many chips you hold
whyNow: Timeless: bubble and final-table spots come up in poker discussion communities every week, and the answer is a short sum that few explainers let you move. Not news-bound.

purposeDetail.concept: The independent chip model: a way to turn each player's chips into expected prize money, by treating finishing order as repeated draws where each remaining player is picked in proportion to chips. It shows why chip value is not linear in dollars.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Everyone has heard that you fold aces on the bubble, almost nobody has moved the numbers. Most explainers state one worked example; this one lets the visitor change stacks, prizes and the all-in and see each sum.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious non-experts and casual tournament players who want to understand why 'a chip is a chip' fails in a prize-ladder game. No poker-hand knowledge needed.
prerequisites: A tournament pays prizes by finishing place
misconceptions: Doubling your chips doubles what they are worth in prize money.
A player with half the chips owns half the prize pool.
Published worked examples all give the same dollar figures (they do not: the page computes exactly and shows its sum).
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Moving a slider so one stack doubles and watching its prize-money bar rise by far less than double, while the short stacks gain without risking a chip.
demos: Winner-take-all with two players: chips equal dollars exactly, the one case where the common belief holds.
Three players, 50/30/20 split: drag stacks and compare chip share bars with prize-money bars, with the finishing-order table shown.
The double-up: one stack doubles by taking chips from another and the prize-money gain is compared with the chip gain.
The bubble all-in: pick two stacks, a pot, and see the winning chance a call needs under chip counting versus under the model, and the gap between them.
Where the model is only an approximation: skill, blinds and position are ignored, with a plain list of limits.
checkQuestions: If the prize ladder were flat (everyone paid the same), what would a chip be worth?
Why does the short stack's prize share exceed its chip share?
A medium stack faces an all-in from a bigger stack: does the required winning chance go up or down compared with chip counting, and why?
What does the model leave out that a real table has?

research.summary: The idea is a real, recurring poker-discussion question (why chips are worth less than face value near the money). The model is documented in a university course lecture (MIT OpenCourseWare 15.S50 lecture 6) and many strategy guides; its mechanics (finishing probability proportional to chips, remove the winner, repeat) are the Harville procedure from horse-racing statistics. I reproduced a published 3-player example (500/300/200 chips, 50/30/20 prizes of 100) exactly in a script: 38.39, 32.75, 28.86, but only one guide's numbers were seen (flagged unverified), and another guide's similar example shows about 42% for the big stack, so published figures do not agree and the page must compute and show its own sum. Free browser ICM calculators for final tables already exist, so this is a lesson, not a paywall-clone tool. Search could not reach Reddit, so the brief's thread claim is unconfirmed.

facts.claim: MIT OpenCourseWare course 15.S50 (How to Win at Texas Hold'em, IAP 2016) has a Lecture 6 on the independent chip model, which argues chip value in tournaments is nonlinear and that maximising chip expectation is only an approximation.

The Harville procedure behind ICM: the chance a player finishes first is their chips divided by all chips; remove that player and renormalise to get second place, and so on; equity is the sum of place probability times prize.

A published 3-player example (stacks 500/300/200, prizes 50/30/20 of 100) is reported at 38.39, 32.75 and 28.86; a node script using the procedure above reproduced exactly 38.3929, 32.75 and 28.8571 on 2026-10-13 (a regression check, not an independent oracle).
Another published guide gives a similar 50/30/20-stack example as roughly 42% of the prize money for the big stack and calls it illustrative, so published worked figures differ from the exact sum.
Free browser ICM calculators for final tables with 2 to 9 players exist (as of 2026-10-13, per VIP-Grinders), so the page makes no paywall claim.
Vendor blog example: in a 10-player 100-unit tournament, a 200-chip stack is worth about 184.44 under ICM rather than 200 (payout structure not seen).
Studies of horse-racing data report that Harville-type models overestimate second and third place chances for likely finishers, so ICM is an approximation.

design.coreLoop: Demo, question, aha: each rung shows chips and dollars side by side, the visitor changes one slider, predicts the direction of the gap, then sees the exact sum. A check question follows each rung and the next rung changes one assumption (second prize, more players, an all-in).
sophisticationHooks: Exact enumeration of finishing orders for up to 9 players with the full probability-by-place table shown, no sampling.
Required-winning-chance readout for a bubble all-in: (equity now minus equity if lost) divided by (equity if won minus equity if lost), compared with the chip-counting break-even.
Honest limits panel and a note that published worked examples disagree, with this page's sums shown for checking by hand.
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: 5 rungs, one pure ICM function (up to 9 players, any prize list), an all-in required-equity function, a shown-working table, 4 check questions, a node self-check for 2-player winner-take-all, 3-player 500/300/200 and equal-prize cases. Cut: tournament simulation, hand ranges, blinds, multi-table, saved progress.
risks: Reddit could not be searched here (the search tool refuses that domain), so the brief's claim that a hot thread asks this question was not confirmed; the idea rests on the recurring question, not on a named thread, and the page names no thread or user.

The oracle is the published procedure plus a script check; the worked example's figures came from a single guide's blended search summary (unverified) and a second guide disagrees. The page must say 'computed here' and show its sum; a verifier should open a source with a clean worked example.
ICM is an approximation (skill, blinds, position ignored); the page states this and avoids advice wording: simulated chips, not advice.
Free ICM calculators exist; differentiation is the teaching ladder and the shown working, so the page must stay a lesson and not drift into a calculator.

title: Priority Inversion Lesson
plainSentence: A lesson that shows, on draggable task timelines, how a low-priority task holding a lock can stall an urgent one, and what fixes it.
pitch: Programmers keep asking the difference between a mutex and a semaphore, and the best answer is a story: in 1997 a rover kept rebooting because a lock was held by the wrong task at the wrong time. This lesson replays that bug on a three-task timeline, lets the visitor stretch one task and see the urgent one wait longer and longer, then flips on priority inheritance and watches it recover. A last rung compares a binary semaphore with a mutex.
firstMinute: The first frame already shows three coloured task lanes over time, with the urgent task blocked behind a lock and a red 'reset' marker where its deadline passes. A toggle labelled priority inheritance sits beside it; flipping it replays the same schedule and the urgent task finishes on time. No reading is needed to see the before and after.
conceptsToLearn: A lock lets only one task use shared data at a time, so others wait
whyNow: Timeless: the mutex versus semaphore question is a perennial programming-forum staple and the 1997 incident is a standard teaching case. Not news-bound.

purposeDetail.concept: Priority inversion: when tasks share a lock and are scheduled by priority, a low-priority lock holder can be preempted by medium-priority work, so the urgent task waits for the medium one without ever sharing its lock; priority inheritance boosts the holder while it blocks someone more urgent.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Most explanations of locks stop at 'only one at a time'. Priority inversion is the part that sinks real-time systems, and the mutex versus binary semaphore difference only makes sense once the visitor has seen it.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious programmers and students who have used locks or heard 'mutex vs semaphore' and want the picture, plus anyone who likes engineering failure stories.
prerequisites: A lock lets one task at a time use shared data
misconceptions: A binary semaphore is just a mutex with a count of one.
A lock can only delay an urgent task by the length of the other task's critical section (without inheritance the delay can be unbounded).
Having a lock means the urgent task always runs first once the lock is free.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Stretching the medium-priority task, which never touches the lock, and watching the urgent task's wait grow with it; then switching inheritance on and seeing the wait shrink to just the lock holder's short section.
demos: Two tasks, one lock: the second waits (the only prerequisite concept).
Three tasks by priority with a shared lock: the bug replays, the urgent task misses its deadline and a watchdog marker fires.
Stretch the medium task: the urgent task's wait grows without limit.
Switch priority inheritance on: the holder is boosted, the wait is only its critical section.
Switch to a priority ceiling and to a plain binary semaphore: see which protects and which does not boost.
checkQuestions: Which task runs while the urgent one waits, and why does it not need the lock?
With inheritance on, what priority does the lock holder run at while the urgent task is blocked on it?
Why does a signalling semaphore not give the holder a boost?
What is the longest the urgent task can now wait?

research.summary: The 1997 rover reset story is documented first-hand by a JPL software lead and by several course notes: a low-priority weather task held a lock a high-priority bus task needed, a medium-priority communications task kept preempting the holder, a watchdog reset the system, and the fix was turning on the lock's priority-inheritance option, patched remotely. The formal result (unbounded inversion with ordinary locks, inheritance and ceiling protocols as fixes) comes from the 1990 Sha, Rajkumar and Lehoczky paper, also covered by encyclopedia and lecture material. The binary-semaphore-is-a-mutex misconception is described in tutorials, with the caveat that the ownership explanation is itself oversimplified, so the lesson teaches intent and priority inheritance and does not claim a universal ownership rule. Reddit was not reachable by search, so no thread was seen.

facts.claim: In the 1997 Mars Pathfinder resets, a low-priority meteorological task held a lock needed by a high-priority bus task, a medium-priority communications task kept preempting the holder, a watchdog forced system resets, and the fix enabled the lock's priority-inheritance flag, changed remotely on the spacecraft.

Sha, Rajkumar and Lehoczky (IEEE Transactions on Computers, 1990) show that ordinary synchronisation primitives allow a higher-priority job to be blocked by lower-priority jobs for an unbounded time; basic priority inheritance removes the unbounded case but can chain blocking; the priority ceiling protocol bounds blocking to one critical section of a lower-priority task and prevents deadlock.

A binary semaphore is commonly taken to be a mutex with a count of one, but tutorials distinguish them by intent (guarding shared state versus signalling) and note that the ownership distinction is implementation-dependent, so it is not a universal rule.

Textbook definition: a semaphore is an integer object with wait (decrement, block if negative) and post (increment, wake one waiter); its initial value sets its behaviour, and a negative value equals the number of waiting threads (OSTEP chapter 31, as summarised by search).
Priority inheritance temporarily raises the priority of a lock holder to that of the highest-priority task blocked on it.

title: Palette Collision Checker
plainSentence: A checker that lets you paste chart colours and see which pairs look alike to colour-blind viewers, then nudges them apart.
pitch: Paste the 3 to 8 colours of a chart or a brand palette and the page shows, for every pair, the worst-case perceptual distance across normal vision and three kinds of colour blindness, as a head-to-head matrix with the numbers shown. Pairs that collapse are flagged in red; one button nudges only the offending colours by the smallest lightness and chroma change until every pair clears a threshold you can set, and the result exports as hex and CSS variables. Everything runs in the browser, nothing is uploaded.
firstMinute: The page opens with a sample 6-colour chart palette already analysed: a strip of swatches, the same strip as seen with red-green and blue-yellow colour blindness, and a pair matrix where two cells glow red because those colours merge. Pressing Fix turns the red cells green and shows what changed in each colour, with no reading needed. Pasting your own hex codes replaces the sample instantly.
conceptsToLearn: Some people cannot tell apart colours that look clearly different to others, so a chart needs colours that differ in lightness as well as hue
whyNow: Timeless: every dashboard and chart needs a categorical palette, and colour-blindness checks are usually done by eye on a screenshot. Not news-bound.

purposeDetail.job: Find the colour pairs in a palette that become indistinguishable under colour-vision deficiency, show the measured distance for each pair, and repair them with the smallest change.
purposeDetail.audience: Designers, analysts and developers who pick colours for charts, maps, UI states and brand palettes and have no quick way to test them beyond eyeballing a simulator.

paywallEvidence.product: A design-plugin accessibility suite (colour-blindness simulator and contrast checker)
paywallEvidence.whatIsGated: Reportedly the free tier simulates 3 deficiency types and the paid tier all 8, at about 15 USD a month; from older vendor material and one review, unconfirmed for today

purposeDetail.freeGap: Free options already simulate colour blindness and flag look-alike colours (a free palette evaluator does this and exports values). The remaining gap is a private, offline page that shows its working as a pair-by-pair distance table, tests against all three dichromacies at once, checks each colour against a chosen background, and proposes a minimal repair instead of leaving the fix to the visitor. The page must not claim to replace any of them, and the paywall claim is unverified and never re...
purposeDetail.oracle: The supplementary CIEDE2000 test data of Sharma, Wu and Dalal (2005), published by the first author as plain-text rows of reference and sample CIELAB values with the expected colour difference; plus the colour-vision-deficiency matrices of Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes (2009).
purposeDetail.inputs: 3 to 8 hex colours (typed, pasted from a list, or picked), an optional background colour, a distance threshold.
purposeDetail.outputs: A pair matrix of worst-case colour difference, simulated strips for normal vision, protan, deutan and tritan, contrast ratio against the background, a repaired palette; exports as a hex list, CSS custom properties and a PNG strip.
purposeDetail.limits: Simulations are models of full dichromacy, not of every person; there is no accepted universal distance threshold, so the default is a labelled convention; it does not test text legibility, patterns or shape cues, and is a screening aid, not a certification.

research.summary: Colour-difference maths is standardised and testable: CIEDE2000 has a published supplementary test set by Sharma, Wu and Dalal that exposes common implementation errors, and the Machado et al. 2009 model supplies the colour-vision-deficiency matrices that open-source libraries reuse. Free palette evaluators exist (one flags look-alike colours under simulated deficiencies), so the idea wins on being private, offline, numeric and repairing, not on novelty of the simulator. No published minimum distance for colour-blind-safe categorical palettes was found; the threshold is a convention and the page says so. Fetching pages failed, so all evidence is from search results.

title: How Letters Get Spaced
plainSentence: A lesson that shows, with draggable letters, how type designers space letters by equalising white area and when a pair still needs kerning.
pitch: Start by fixing an ugly word with a tracking slider and one kerning drag, then discover why the same distance between letter edges looks different for HH, HO and AV: what the eye reads is the white area. A ladder of small demos built on a typeface drawn in code lets the visitor space letters by area, watch the rhythm of a row of n and o, blur the text to see its grey tone, and learn which pairs spacing cannot fix.
firstMinute: The page opens on the word AVOID set with default spacing, with the gap between A and V shaded so the hole is visible, and a tracking slider plus a draggable pair handle. Dragging the V towards the A closes the hole and the shaded area number drops, which is the first success with no reading.
conceptsToLearn: Every letter sits in a box with a little space on each side; the gap you see between two letters is the sum of those two spaces
whyNow: Timeless: anyone who sets headlines, logos or slides meets uneven letter gaps. Type spacing is a niche most people have never been shown properly.

purposeDetail.concept: Letter spacing is set by the white area between letters, not by the distance between their edges; kerning is a patch for the few pairs that spacing cannot fix.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: People know the words kerning and tracking but rarely see how a type designer sets the space on each side of every letter first, or why diagonal and round letters break the rules.
purposeDetail.audience: Designers, students, slide-makers and curious readers; no design knowledge needed.
misconceptions: Kerning and tracking are the same thing.
Uneven spacing is fixed by adding kerning pairs everywhere.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Two pairs with identical edge-to-edge distance, H next to H and A next to V, look nothing alike, and the shaded white areas show why; closing the area, not the distance, evens the row.
demos: 1. Tracking against kerning: a slider moves every gap, a handle moves one pair.
2. Same distance, different area: shaded gaps for HH, HO, OO and AV with live area numbers.
3. Space by area: set one target area and see sidebearings computed for a small geometric typeface drawn from shapes, with an n-and-o rhythm strip.
4. Blur test: a squint slider shows the grey tone of a line before and after spacing.
5. What spacing cannot fix: AV, To and WA, where a hand-set kerning pair is the right tool.
checkQuestions: If you tighten every gap in a headline equally, are you tracking or kerning?
Which pair needs more care at equal edge distance: HH or AV, and why?
After spacing by area, one pair still looks open. What is the right fix?

research.summary: The lesson rests on how type designers space fonts. Foundry guidance says to fix spacing through each glyph's side spaces first and use kerning only for pairs that remain awkward. Spacing guides describe judging letters against a fence of n or m and aiming for an even grey tone. An open area-based spacing script equalises the white area and depth per letter group but does not kern and does not replace the eye. Kerning and tracking are widely confused. The typeface will be drawn in code from shapes, so no font file is used. Page fetching failed, so everything is from search results.

facts.claim: Kerning adjusts the space of one specific letter pair; tracking (also called letter-spacing) changes the spacing of a whole run of text.
Kerning and tracking are frequently confused with each other.
Foundry guidance says spacing problems should not be fixed by adding kerning pairs: set sidebearings first, then kern the exceptions.
Type designers commonly judge spacing against a fence of n or m letters and aim for an even grey value; only the x-height zone matters for roman lowercase.
An open area-based spacing tool equalises the white area and depth of letters per group, does not kern, and does not replace a designer's eye.
A letter's bounding box ignores its shape, so diagonal and round letters (A-V, T-o, W-A) leave uneven gaps that need kerning.

design.coreLoop: Demo, question, aha: see a flaw, move a handle or slider to remove it, read the number that changes, then answer a check question whose answer follows from the same model; each rung adds one idea.
sophisticationHooks: A geometric typeface of about 12 letters drawn in code from rectangles, circles and polygons, so area is computed exactly and no font file is used
Live white-area readout between neighbours inside the x-height zone, capped by depth

design.scopeForOneDay: Built: glyph set as SVG paths, area-between-glyphs routine (raster on an offscreen canvas, fixed resolution), five demos, three check questions with computed answers, intro and glossary. Cut: real font loading, full alphabet, export of a font, language-specific rules.
risks: Area equalisation is a simplified model of a judgement-based craft; the page must say it is a model and that real fonts are finished by eye.
Kerning and tracking confusion is documented by a course page and a FontShop article, but the summary attributing it was blended, so the page words it as widely reported.
The A-L-T-V-W-Y claim was seen only in a blended summary and is not stated as fact.
The page must not name tools or foundries as endorsements; the method is described in its own words and credited generically.
Brief's claim of measurable physics holds for contrast and colour difference; spacing is partly perceptual and the lesson shows that honestly.

title: PDF Page Arranger
plainSentence: A tool that lets you merge PDFs, keep chosen pages, reorder, rotate and number them, all inside your browser with nothing uploaded.
pitch: Drop one or more PDFs onto the page and every page becomes a card showing its size, rotation and first words. Drag cards into a new order, delete or rotate them, type a range such as 1-3,7,9- to keep only some, optionally stamp 'Page 3 of 12' numbers, and download the new file. A printed check strip then re-reads the output with a second parser and reports its page count and whether each page's text matches the input.
firstMinute: On load two small sample documents are already merged into five page cards, with a finished check strip beneath them that types itself out like teleprinter paper (page count 5, text matches). One button, 'Download PDF', gives a working file without reading anything; dragging a card or pressing Rotate updates the strip instantly.
whyNow: Timeless. Merging and reordering pages is a weekly chore, and free web suites commonly meter it (a per-hour or per-day task cap, a size cap, or an account), so a private, unlimited, offline version keeps being useful.

purposeDetail.job: Combine, extract, reorder, rotate and page-number the pages of unencrypted PDF files, producing one new PDF that is re-read and checked before the visitor downloads it.
purposeDetail.audience: Anyone who occasionally assembles a PDF from several files (forms, scans, receipts, a thesis, a legal or school packet) and does not want to upload private documents or hit a daily cap.

paywallEvidence.product: A large web PDF suite (named in the dossier only, never on the page)
paywallEvidence.whatIsGated: Its own pricing page sells a Premium plan that lists unlimited document processing and no ads, at 5 USD a month billed annually or 9 USD billed monthly, as of 2026-10-13; the free tier is therefore limited.

paywallEvidence.product: A second web PDF suite (dossier only)
paywallEvidence.whatIsGated: Third-party listings report about two free tasks a day and a small free file-size cap, with a paid plan lifting them. One reviewer reports one document a day, and no official page was seen, so this stays unverified and is not shown as fact.

purposeDetail.freeGap: Free in-browser mergers already exist (some self-describe as pdf-lib based and offline-capable), so privacy alone is not new. The remaining gap is an all-five-jobs page that is exact and shows its working: a second-parser check strip (page count, per-page text match), page-number stamping that respects rotation and crop boxes, known-answer tests against the PDF standard, and loud, specific refusals (encrypted, damaged or exotic files) instead of silent breakage.
purposeDetail.oracle: ISO 32000-1:2008 (PDF 1.7), free from the publisher of the format via the PDF Association: file structure (cross-reference table, trailer, page tree and inheritable attributes, the Rotate rule). Plus round-trip checks: page count and extracted text of each output page must equal the chosen input page.
purposeDetail.inputs: One or more PDF files from disk (drag and drop or file picker), a page-range text such as 1-3,7,9-, per-card rotate and delete, drag order, and optional page-number settings (position, start, 'of N').
purposeDetail.outputs: A downloaded PDF (1.4-style classic cross-reference table written by the page itself), plus a copyable plain-text check receipt.
purposeDetail.limits: Printed on the page: encrypted or password-protected files, files with a damaged cross-reference table, and signed documents are refused or lose their signature; form fields, links, bookmarks and tagged-structure data are dropped from copied pages; page thumbnails are text summaries, not rendered images; very large files are limited by browser memory.

research.summary: The job is real and metered: one large suite's own pricing page sells unlimited processing as Premium, third-party listings describe daily or hourly free caps, but free client-side mergers exist, so the build must win on exactness and visible checking. The standard is free to read (ISO 32000-1 via Adobe, 32000-2 via the PDF Association), the tricky parts are known (page-tree inheritance of Resources, MediaBox, CropBox and Rotate; xref entries of 20 bytes; xref streams and object streams in PDF 1.5 and later), and the browser now offers deflate decompression natively, so no vendored library is required.

title: Inside a PDF File
plainSentence: A lesson that shows how a PDF file finds its pages, and why deleted content can stay inside it, with editable demos.
pitch: The lesson opens a tiny PDF as plain, line-numbered text on teleprinter-style paper and walks a ladder of five editable demos: object numbers, the cross-reference table of byte offsets, the page tree that sets page order, appended revisions that keep old content, and why a black box is not a delete key. Each rung changes a live file and shows what a reader would do, and two or more self-check questions apply the rules to new files.
firstMinute: A three-line-page PDF is already open in the left pane as text, and the right pane shows the page it draws. Clicking any numbered object lights up its bytes and its entry in the offset table; changing one word of the page text redraws the page and recomputes every offset on screen.
conceptsToLearn: A PDF is a file made of numbered objects that you can read as text.
whyNow: Timeless. Failed black-box redactions and 'deleted' text surviving in files are recurring stories, and almost nobody has seen the structure that explains them.

purposeDetail.concept: How a PDF is organised: numbered objects, a cross-reference table that maps object numbers to byte offsets, a page tree that decides page order, and append-only revisions that explain why 'deleted' or 'blacked out' content can still be in the file.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: People use PDFs daily and trust them to hide things, yet the file layout is rarely shown. Seeing the offsets and the appended revision turns folklore into a mental model.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious non-experts, students, and anyone who redacts or edits documents before sharing them.
misconceptions: Deleting text in a PDF editor removes it from the file.
Drawing a black box over text removes the text.
Pages appear in the order their objects sit in the file.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Pressing 'show revision 1' on a file whose text was 'deleted' brings the old words back from the same bytes, and extracting text under a black box returns it.
demos: Overture: the smallest legal one-page file as numbered lines; click an object to see its bytes
Offsets: edit the text and watch every cross-reference entry recompute; break one on purpose and see the mismatch flagged
Page tree: reorder the Kids list and see the pages swap while the object bytes stay put
Revisions: delete a line, see the appended update with its Prev pointer, then view the file as of revision 1
Black box versus removal: draw a box, extract text, then actually drop the text and compare
checkQuestions: Given a short file listing, what number belongs in the startxref line and why?
Given a Kids list and object order, which page is first?
Given a file with two revisions, is the 'deleted' word still present, and where?
After a black box is drawn over a name, what does text extraction return?

research.summary: Appended revisions, black-box redaction failures and page-tree ordering are all documented outside the standard, and the file-layout facts (startxref, xref entries, trailer Root, Prev chain) are described consistently by independent references, with the free ISO text as the named authority. The lesson can be built from tiny files authored in code, so no third-party documents are bundled.

facts.claim: A PDF incremental update appends new objects, a new cross-reference section and a trailer with a Prev pointer to the end of the file; readers show the newest revision while earlier bytes remain in the file and can be recovered.

Drawing a black rectangle over text in many PDF editors adds a graphic on top and leaves the underlying text in the file, where it can still be selected or extracted; real redaction deletes the content.
Per one publisher's article only, page order comes from the Kids array of the page tree rather than from object numbers or their position in the file; not independently confirmed.

A reader finds the file's structure from the end: startxref gives the byte offset of the last cross-reference section, whose 20-byte entries (10-digit offset, 5-digit generation, n or f) lead to the trailer's Root and the page tree.
ISO 32000-1 (PDF 1.7) is free from Adobe as listed by the PDF Association, and ISO 32000-2 (PDF 2.0) is free through the PDF Association's sponsored-standards page.

title: Why Flat Maps Distort
plainSentence: A lesson that lets you drag countries on a world map and watch their size change, to see why flat maps always distort something.
pitch: Drag Greenland down a Mercator map and watch it shrink beside Africa, then switch to other projections with Tissot's circles drawn on them and plot a flight that is curved on one map and straight on another. A ladder of six small demos and check-yourself questions busts the idea that one map is the true one and ends on the point that every map is an argument. Made for travellers and geography fans, no maths needed, all offline.
firstMinute: The page opens on a Mercator world map where a ghost-ember copy of Greenland already slides toward Africa and shrinks, with the caption that it is the same country with the same true area. The visitor drags Greenland themself and sees a live 'drawn size vs true size' readout fall to 1x at the equator. No reading is needed for that first success.
conceptsToLearn: a map is a flat picture of a ball, so some stretching is unavoidable
whyNow: Timeless: the Greenland-versus-Africa picture is a perennial map-geek topic and a hot spot of a classroom misconception; the lens brief and a 2026 article on the Greenland versus Mercator size comparison show it is still discussed.

purposeDetail.concept: A sphere cannot be flattened without distorting something. A projection chooses what to keep: Mercator keeps angles (conformal) and so stretches lengths by sec(latitude) and areas by sec squared (4 times at 60 degrees, about 33 times at 80); equal-area maps keep area and bend shapes; no projection can be both conformal and equal-area; great circles are straight only on a gnomonic map.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Usual explanations are either a static 'Mercator is bad' infographic or a true-size drag toy with no why: nobody shows the area-scale curve, the Tissot circles and the great-circle flight together, or says that Mercator is excellent at its actual job (straight compass courses).
purposeDetail.audience: Curious travellers, geography fans, students and anyone who has argued about Greenland on a world map.
prerequisites: what latitude and longitude are, roughly
misconceptions: The map on the classroom wall (Mercator) shows true country sizes.
There is one correct projection and the others are wrong.
The straight line on a map is the shortest route.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Dragging the same Tissot circle from the equator to the Arctic: on Mercator it stays round but swells to many times its size, on the equal-area map it keeps its size but flattens into an ellipse, and you realise you can never keep both.
demos: Rung 1: drag Greenland (and any country) across a Mercator map with a live drawn-size-over-true-size readout and a ghost showing home size.
Rung 2: the stretch dial: slide a latitude marker and see the sec-squared area multiplier (1x, 2x, 4x at 60 degrees, about 33x at 80) beside a row of identical true-size circles.
Rung 3: Tissot's circles on a gallery of five projections (Mercator, plain equirectangular, equal-area cylindrical, sinusoidal, azimuthal) with a shape-error and area-error meter.
Rung 4: the trade-off slider: morph Mercator toward an equal-area map and watch the two errors trade places but never both reach zero.
Rung 5: pick two cities and fly the shortest route: curved on Mercator, straight on a gnomonic view, with the constant-compass-heading line (rhumb line) for contrast.
Rung 6: 'argue with a map': match jobs (sailing course, country sizes, polar flights) to the projection that serves them.
checkQuestions: On a Mercator map, by about what factor is the area of a small shape at 60 degrees latitude exaggerated? (4)
Africa is roughly how many times Greenland's real area? (about 14)
On an equal-area map, what happens to a Tissot circle near the edge? (same area, becomes an ellipse)
What does a great-circle flight look like on a gnomonic map? (a straight line)
Why can't a map be both equal-area and conformal? (curvature of a sphere cannot be flattened without losing one)

research.summary: Searches confirm the core mathematics (Mercator is conformal, rhumb lines straight, scale grows as the secant of latitude, so area as its square), the Tissot behaviour per class of projection (circles stay round but grow on conformal maps, keep area but become ellipses on equal-area maps), and the standard Greenland-versus-Africa teaching case (Africa about 14 times Greenland by area, Greenland about one eighth of South America). The 'one projection is the true one' misconception is documented only in informal sources (an essay by a graphic designer about 'immappancy', a development-education article), not a controlled study. Great circles straight on a gnomonic map and curved on Mercator is stated by navigation sources. My own node computations agree: secant squared is 4.00 at 60 degrees, 8.55 at 70 and 33.16 at 80; Africa over Greenland is 14.0; Greenland over South America is 0.121, about one eighth.

facts.claim: On conformal maps (Mercator) Tissot circles stay circles but change size; on equal-area maps they keep their area but turn into ellipses; on a globe all are equal circles.
Mercator is conformal, its equator has constant scale, and a rhumb line (constant heading) is a straight line on it; PROJ calls it inappropriate for world maps.
Mercator stretches lengths along a parallel by sec(latitude), so area scales by sec squared: 4 times at 60 degrees, about 8.5 at 70, about 33 at 80 (computed with node: 4.00, 8.55, 33.16).

Greenland's area is about 2.17 million square km and Africa's about 30.4 million, a ratio of about 14 (computed 14.0); Greenland is about one eighth of South America (computed 0.121). Source is low authority: show as approximate.
No map projection can be both equal-area and conformal (Gauss's Theorema Egregium; Euler attribution is secondary).
Great circles are curves on a Mercator map where straight lines are rhumb lines; a gnomonic map shows great circles as straight lines.
The belief that Mercator shows true country sizes (people misjudging Africa against Greenland) is documented in informal essays and an education article, not in a controlled study.

title: Shortest Route Calculator
plainSentence: A calculator that compares the shortest route between two places with the straight-line course on a flat map, giving distances, headings and waypoints.
pitch: Pick two places from a bundled list or type coordinates, and see the great-circle distance, the constant-heading (rhumb line) distance, the extra distance the straight-on-the-map course costs, and how the compass heading changes along the shortest route. Two small maps show the same trip on Mercator and on a gnomonic view, and the waypoints (every N km) can be copied as a plain list. Everything runs in the browser and shows its formulas.
firstMinute: The page opens with a sample trip, Los Angeles to Tokyo, already computed: 8,753 km along the great circle against 9,236 km along the straight course, about 5.5 percent more. The curved route and the straight line are drawn on the Mercator map, and the visitor swaps either end to see the numbers change instantly.
whyNow: Timeless utility for travellers, pilots-in-training, sailors and trivia lovers; it pairs with the map-distortion lesson but works alone.

purposeDetail.job: Compute, for any two points on Earth, the great-circle distance and bearings, the rhumb-line distance and constant bearing, the percentage penalty of the rhumb line, and evenly spaced waypoints along either path.
purposeDetail.audience: Travellers curious why flights curve, student pilots and sailors learning route planning, teachers, trivia and map fans.
purposeDetail.freeGap: Free options already do the core job: a popular web mapper gives great-circle distances for multi-stop routes and a free calculator compares great-circle with rhumb routes and generates waypoints. No paywall was found, so the real remaining gap is: fully private and offline, formulas and every step shown, side-by-side Mercator and gnomonic pictures, and an honest sphere-error note.
purposeDetail.oracle: Exact identities on the sphere (radius 6371.0088 km): a quarter meridian is pi/2 times R = 10007.54 km; a degree of longitude on the equator is 111.195 km; a rhumb along a parallel is cos(latitude) times longitude difference times R; the rhumb equals the great circle along a meridian; antipodes are pi times R apart. Plus a worked pair, Los Angeles to Tokyo, whose published values (8754 and 9236 km) my own haversine and rhumb code reproduce (8753 and 9236).
purposeDetail.inputs: Two places (bundled list of about 150 cities or typed latitude and longitude in decimal degrees), waypoint spacing, radius choice (mean sphere).
purposeDetail.outputs: Distances in km, miles and nautical miles; initial, final and rhumb bearings; percent penalty; midpoint; waypoint list as plain text rows; two small SVG maps.
purposeDetail.limits: Spherical Earth only, so distances can be off by up to about 0.3 to 0.5 percent against the true ellipsoid; no land, airspace, weather or wind; not for navigation; paths crossing the antimeridian are handled by wrapping longitude; the gnomonic view cannot show points more than 90 degrees from its centre.

research.summary: The method is textbook: haversine for great-circle distance, the standard initial-bearing formula and the isometric-latitude formula for rhumb lines. The author of the best-known reference scripts states that spherical formulas are accurate to about 0.3 percent, and an encyclopedia states about 0.5 percent. Free competitors exist (a popular great-circle mapper for flights, a route calculator that compares great circle and rhumb and lists waypoints), so no paywall is claimed. A navigation note says great circles only save much when both ends are above about 45 degrees and far apart; my own computation shows Los Angeles to Tokyo costs 5.5 percent on the rhumb line, New York to London 3.9 percent, Los Angeles to Sydney 0.3 percent.

title: Nonogram Puzzle Checker
plainSentence: A nonogram maker that lets you draw a picture, get its number clues, and check whether anyone can solve it without guessing.
pitch: Draw a picture on a small grid and the page writes the number clues around it, like a picture-by-numbers puzzle. It then solves the puzzle the way a person would, one row or column at a time, and reports whether the clues have exactly one answer and whether the whole grid falls out without guessing. If it does not, it shades the stuck squares and suggests a one-square change that repairs it; then you print the puzzle sheet and an answer page.
firstMinute: A 10 by 10 sample picture is already drawn with its clues written around it, and a slow replay is solving it pass by pass in colour. A verdict card reads something like 'One answer, no guessing needed, 6 passes, easy'. Click a single square to flip it and watch the verdict change, perhaps to 'Two answers' with the ambiguous squares shaded.
conceptsToLearn: A nonogram is a picture-by-numbers grid: each number says how long a run of filled squares is in that row or column.
whyNow: Timeless: anyone who makes puzzles for a book, a class or a friend hits the same trap, a puzzle that has one answer on paper but forces guessing. The page makes that visible in seconds.

purposeDetail.job: Turn a drawn picture into nonogram clues and prove, with visible working, whether the puzzle has exactly one answer and can be finished by row-and-column logic alone.
purposeDetail.audience: Puzzle makers, teachers, parents and hobbyists who want to design nonograms that are fair to solve, and solvers curious why a puzzle got stuck.

paywallEvidence.product: A paid no-guess nonogram toolkit sold through a small-seller storefront
paywallEvidence.whatIsGated: The check that every accepted puzzle can be finished by row-and-column logic alone, plus the print-ready puzzle-book PDF with answer pages; listed at 29 US dollars as of 2026-10-13, per the seller's own listing.

purposeDetail.freeGap: Free editors exist that check solvability or uniqueness (search results mention an in-game checker on a fan wiki and an open-source editor still in development), so uniqueness alone is not the gap. Not confirmed that any free one tests the stricter no-guess property, shows each solving pass, and proposes a one-square repair. The real remaining gap is: private, in the browser, shows its working, suggests the fix. Unverified for any named free tool; the page will not compare itself to any product.
purposeDetail.oracle: Published counts of small square nonograms: the number of n by n grids whose clues give a unique solution that row-and-column logic alone can finish, from OEIS entry A391619 (1, 2, 14, 384, 51234, 24976511 for sizes 0 to 5); the broader unique-solution counts are in OEIS A242876. The built-in self-test enumerates every grid up to 4 by 4 and compares.
purposeDetail.inputs: A picture drawn by clicking or dragging on a grid from 5 by 5 to 15 by 15 (20 by 20 under More), or pasted clue numbers; a sample picture is preloaded.
purposeDetail.outputs: Clue numbers, a verdict (no solution, several solutions, one solution needing guesses, or one solution reached by logic alone), a difficulty label from the pass count, the stuck squares, a suggested one-square repair, and exports: puzzle sheet and answer page as PNG, SVG and a print layout, plus a share link holding the grid.
purposeDetail.limits: Black-and-white nonograms only, up to 20 by 20. Exhaustive checking of larger grids is capped and reported as 'could not decide' rather than guessed. Difficulty is a rough label from solving passes, not a verdict on how hard a person will find it. No photo import.

research.summary: Uniqueness and no-guess solvability are different properties. A seller of a paid toolkit says most nonogram generators check nothing or only uniqueness, while its own accepted puzzles must be finished by working one row or column at a time. The count of 5 by 5 grids that are unique and line-solvable (24,976,511 of 33,554,432) is documented, and a gap of hundreds of thousands of grids are unique but need guessing. Uniqueness checking is NP-hard in general, but a line solver is cheap and a cap on the exhaustive search keeps the page fast. That makes a faithful, auditable, in-browser checker with a repair suggestion realistic in one morning.

title: Exact Cover Lesson
plainSentence: A lesson that shows how a computer fits shapes into a board by trying, undoing and counting every way, step by step.
pitch: Watch a slow-motion solver tile small boards with dominoes and pentominoes, then take the controls: pick the next piece yourself, see the dead end, back up, and watch a counter tick up as every tiling is found. A glowing marker always points at the square with the fewest options, and you learn why that one rule tames the search. The last rung shows that sudoku is the same kind of problem, so a puzzle designer can ask 'does it have exactly one answer?' by counting to two.
firstMinute: A small board is already being tiled by a slow-motion solver: pieces drop in, a dead end appears, the pieces lift out, and a counter shows 'tilings found: 3'. A glowing marker sits on the square with the fewest options. Press Step to advance the solver yourself; the first success is seeing it hit a dead end, back up and find a full tiling.
conceptsToLearn: Exact cover means every square is covered by exactly one piece: no gaps, no overlaps.
whyNow: Timeless. The same tiny idea sits behind pentomino puzzles, sudoku solvers and scheduling, and few people see that it is one idea.

purposeDetail.concept: Exact cover: choose from a list of allowed placements so that every square is covered exactly once, and how a backtracking solver finds, and counts, all the ways by always branching on the most constrained square.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: It is the hidden common core of pentomino tilings, sudoku, and scheduling puzzles, yet most people meet it only as 'a clever linked-list trick'. Seeing the table of placements makes the trick obvious.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious puzzle fans, students meeting backtracking, and anyone who has wondered how a sudoku solver can prove a puzzle has only one answer.
misconceptions: A puzzle solver just tries every combination until one works.
Tiling puzzles and sudoku are unrelated families of puzzle.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Re-draw the board as a table where each row is one legal placement and each column is one thing that must be covered once; solving is just picking rows with exactly one tick in every column. Then the same table solves a sudoku.
demos: Rung 1: slow-motion solver tiling a small board with dominoes; step, undo, and a counter of tilings found
Rung 2: you pick pieces by hand and the page lights the beacon on the tightest square; compare your tries with the solver's
Rung 3: the table view, rows as placements and columns as squares, with choose, cover and undo highlighted
Rung 4: a board with two opposite corners removed, where the solver proves zero tilings; and the 6 by 10 pentomino board counted live against the published total
Rung 5: sudoku redrawn as the same table, and 'count to two' as a uniqueness check on a puzzle the visitor edits
checkQuestions: If a square has zero legal placements left, what must the solver do, and why is that good news for speed?
Why does picking the square with the fewest options first usually shrink the search?
A sudoku solver finds one answer. What else must it check before saying the puzzle has exactly one?
In the table view, what does it mean when a column has no rows left?

research.summary: Exact cover is documented as the common formulation of pentomino tilings and sudoku, with Knuth's Algorithm X as a recursive depth-first backtracking search made fast by Dancing Links. The 6 by 10 pentomino board has a published total of 2,339 tilings (counted up to rotating or flipping the whole board), a strong known-answer check for an in-page solver. The most-constrained-first rule is documented both in Norvig's well-known sudoku essay and in algorithm tutorials. The designer's question, how few clues still give one answer, ties to a published exhaustive search showing no 16-clue sudoku exists.

facts.claim: Pentomino tilings and sudoku are both standard examples of exact cover problems, and Knuth's Algorithm X is a recursive depth-first backtracking search that finds all solutions; Dancing Links is its fast implementation.
Knuth's Dancing Links paper uses placing pentominoes as its running example.
The 6 by 10 rectangle can be tiled by the 12 pentominoes in 2,339 ways, counting rotations and reflections of the whole board as the same.
Good solvers branch first on the square or constraint with the fewest remaining options, which reduces branching compared with trying squares in a fixed order.
A 2012 exhaustive computer search found no 16-clue sudoku with a unique solution, so 17 clues is the minimum known to be needed.

Sudoku as exact cover has 729 candidate placements and 324 things to cover once (81 cells plus digit-in-row, digit-in-column and digit-in-box pairs); reported in a blended search summary, not attributed to a single page.

title: Cron DST Night Rehearsal
plainSentence: A checker that lets you enter a cron line and a time zone and see which runs vanish or double on the two daylight-saving nights.
pitch: The visitor enters a five-field cron line and picks an IANA time zone. The page draws the spring-forward and fall-back nights as a minute timeline and marks every run under two named rules: the literal wall-clock rule in crontab(5) (skipped time never fires, repeated time fires twice) and the classic cron(8) rule (a skipped fixed-time job fires right after the jump, a repeated one fires once). Each run shows local time, UTC and offset, so a nightly 02:30 job is seen vanishing in New York in March and doubling in November. It runs offline from the browser's zone data, with no account or upload, and prints its limits.
firstMinute: The page opens with a sample line (30 2 * * *) in America/New_York and the March spring-forward night already drawn: the 02:30 run is marked as lost under the wall-clock rule and as run at 03:00 under the classic rule. One click on the fall-back tab shows the 01:30 run counted twice versus once, so the first success needs no reading.
conceptsToLearn: A cron line has five fields: minute, hour, day of month, month, day of week
whyNow: Clocks go back in the EU and UK on 2026-10-25 and in the US on 2026-11-01, so people with nightly jobs are about to meet the repeated hour; the tool stays useful every March and October.

purposeDetail.job: Show what a five-field cron line does on the two clock-change nights of one IANA zone, under two named scheduler rules, with local time, UTC and offset for every run.
purposeDetail.audience: Developers, sysadmins and data engineers with nightly or hourly jobs who need to know whether a job will be lost or doubled at a daylight-saving change, without trusting a next-runs list that ignores the jump.

paywallEvidence.product: Pay-per-use cron expression parser services listed on a cloud automation marketplace
paywallEvidence.whatIsGated: Metered API calls that return next fire times; listings advertise time zone awareness, but none shown in the results draws the daylight-saving nights or compares scheduler rules

purposeDetail.freeGap: Free options exist: next-run testers need no signup and an open-source library claims DST support. The real gap is that none seen shows the two clock-change nights as a timeline, compares the literal and the classic rule, shows its working per run, or runs offline with no upload. Not a paywalled job as such; the value is private, offline and explanatory.
purposeDetail.oracle: The crontab(5) and cron(8) manual pages (Linux man-pages, OpenBSD, NetBSD, Debian cronie wording) for the two rules, plus hand-made transition calendars for a few zones (New York, London, Lord Howe, Sydney) written from published transition dates.
purposeDetail.inputs: A five-field cron line (with lists, ranges, steps and month or weekday names), an IANA zone chosen from a bundled list, and a choice of year and of spring or fall night.
purposeDetail.outputs: A minute-level timeline of the chosen night, a table of every run with local time, UTC and offset under each rule, a one-line verdict (lost, doubled, shifted, unchanged), and a copyable plain-text report.
purposeDetail.limits: Dialects differ and the page cannot know which scheduler the visitor runs; it models two documented rules only. Not modelled: systemd timers, cloud schedulers, Quartz, jobs started late by a busy machine, and clock changes of three hours or more (which cron(8) treats as clock corrections). Zone data comes from the visitor's browser and may lag the newest tzdata release.

research.summary: The two named rules are real and documented separately. The Linux crontab(5) page says times that do not exist never match and times that occur twice run matching jobs twice; the cron(8) pages (OpenBSD, Debian cronie, NetBSD) say clock changes under three hours get special handling for fixed-time or longer-than-hourly jobs: skipped ones run immediately after a forward jump, repeated ones are not run twice, and more frequent jobs are scheduled normally. A FreeBSD bug report is titled as a contradiction between the two pages, and the Healthchecks author says their CronSim library follows Debian cron, which shows dialects differ and the tool should say so. Search results suggest free next-run testers do not draw the DST nights; that was not confirmed by opening any of them. The EU and UK change dates for 2026 are confirmed by two results.

The cron(8) manual pages of OpenBSD, Debian cronie and NetBSD say clock changes under three hours are handled specially for fixed-time jobs or granularity above one hour: after a forward change skipped jobs run immediately, after a backward change running a job twice is avoided; more frequent jobs are scheduled normally; changes over three hours are treated as corrections.
A FreeBSD bug report titled as contradicting information in crontab(5) and cron(8) about DST exists, so the two man pages have disagreed on the topic.

The Healthchecks author reports from experiment that Debian cron follows its man page (fixed-time jobs in a skipped hour run after the jump, repeated-hour jobs are not rerun, wildcard jobs keep even intervals), and that their CronSim library copies this behaviour.

Free options exist: an open-source library (CronDst) states support for time zones and DST, and a free browser tester (enterno.io) lists next run times without saying how it treats DST; neither seen draws the two clock-change nights.
As of 2026-10-13, per one marketplace listing (unconfirmed, listings disagree), a pay-per-use cron parser charges per expression parsed.
In 2026 the EU and UK change from summer to winter time on Sunday 2026-10-25 at 01:00 UTC, having started summer time on Sunday 2026-03-29.

title: Skipped And Repeated Times
plainSentence: A lesson that shows, with live clocks, why some local times never happen and others happen twice on daylight-saving nights, and how software should pick.
pitch: A short ladder of interactive demos starts from the familiar sentence 'clocks go forward an hour' and ends at the aha: a wall-clock time is not a single moment. The visitor drags a pointer along the real UTC timeline of a clock-change night and watches the local clock skip 02:30 in March or show 01:30 twice in November, then tries the four ways software resolves such a time (earlier, later, reject, compatible) and meets a half-hour zone. Check-yourself questions end each rung, with answers worked out by the page's own time functions.
firstMinute: The first frame shows a running timeline of New York on 2026-11-01 with two clocks ticking from UTC: the local clock reads 01:30, then 01:30 again an hour later, with the repeat highlighted. A single slider scrubs through the night, so the first success (seeing 01:30 occur twice) takes seconds and needs no reading.
whyNow: Clocks go back in the EU and UK on 2026-10-25 and in the US on 2026-11-01, the two weeks in which this confusion is in the news and in production incidents; the concept itself is timeless.

purposeDetail.concept: A local wall-clock time is not always one instant: on a spring-forward night some local times do not exist (a gap) and on a fall-back night some occur twice (a fold), so software must choose a rule to turn wall-clock time into a moment.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: Programmers learn 'store UTC' but rarely see the gap and the fold as a picture, nor the four standard resolution policies; most explainers list falsehoods without letting the learner poke the timeline.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious people and working developers who schedule, book or log things in local time and have been surprised by a daylight-saving night.
prerequisites: Knowing that clocks change by about an hour for daylight saving time
misconceptions: Every day has 24 hours
Every local time exists exactly once
Daylight saving always shifts clocks by exactly one hour, at the same moment everywhere
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: Scrubbing the UTC slider through the November night and seeing the local clock read 01:30 at two different UTC moments, then seeing the March night skip from 01:59 to 03:00: the local reading is only a label, and the offset is what makes it a moment.
demos: Scrub a UTC slider through a clock-change night in a chosen zone while local and UTC clocks run side by side
Click any local time on a day strip to see how many real moments match it (zero, one or two) and with which offsets
Resolver bench: pick a gap or repeated time and see what earlier, later, reject and compatible each return, with UTC and offset
Day-length demo: add 24 hours versus add one calendar day across the jump and compare
Half-hour zone (Lord Howe) and a southern-hemisphere zone, to bust the 'always one hour, always March and November' belief
checkQuestions: On 2026-11-01 in New York, how many real moments read 01:30, and what are their offsets?
A meeting is booked for 02:30 local on the spring-forward date: which moment does 'compatible' pick, and why might 'reject' be safer?
How long is the calendar day of the fall-back date in hours?
Why can two different UTC moments print the same local time without any error in the clock?

research.summary: The vocabulary and the resolution policies are standardised, not invented. PEP 495 names the two cases (fold for a backward change with ambiguous times, gap for a forward change with missing times) and uses a 0 or 1 flag to choose the earlier or later reading; MDN documents the four Temporal options (compatible, earlier, later, reject, default compatible); library docs (Whenever) give worked gap and fold examples. Falsehoods lists document the misconceptions (24-hour days, same moment everywhere, always an hour). Lord Howe Island's 30-minute shift is documented by two independent results. The IANA tz database page frames the data the demos rest on.

title: Sealed-Bid Auction Lesson
plainSentence: A lesson that lets you bid against simulated rivals in first-price and second-price sealed auctions and see how shading your bid changes your profit.
pitch: You get a private value for an item (say a mug worth 60 play-dollars to you) and bid against four simulated rivals, first in a rising-price auction, then in sealed first-price and second-price versions. A slider shades your bid below or above your value and a profit curve, built from thousands of replayed rounds, shows that shading pays in the first-price auction and never pays in the second-price one. You leave knowing why the rule of the game, not good manners, makes honest bidding the best plan, and exactly when that stops being true.
firstMinute: The first frame already shows an ascending auction running: a price ladder climbs, rivals drop out, and a card says what the item is worth to you. You tap Drop out when the price reaches your value, see you won with a small profit, and see the same round replayed with a higher and a lower dropout point so you can see why leaving at your value was best.
conceptsToLearn: your value for an item is what it is worth to you; profit is value minus the price you pay
whyNow: Timeless. The ad-tech industry's 2019 switch from second-price to first-price auctions made bid shading a live topic, and nobody shows the arithmetic behind it.

purposeDetail.concept: In a sealed-bid second-price auction the highest bidder wins but pays the second-highest bid, so your own bid only decides whether you win, never what you pay; bidding your true value is therefore a dominant strategy when values are private. In a first-price auction you pay what you bid, so you shade below value; with n risk-neutral bidders whose values are independent and uniform on 0 to 1, the equilibrium bid is (n-1)/n of your value.
purposeDetail.whyNiche: It is usually taught as a theorem or as a one-line conclusion, so it sounds like an opinion. Few places let a learner try to cheat the rule and watch it fail, or show that the same honest bid is wrong under a different rule.
purposeDetail.audience: Curious adults, students of economics or computer science, and anyone who has argued about eBay, ad markets or spectrum sales.
prerequisites: subtracting a price from a value
misconceptions: Bidding below my value always saves me money, in any auction.
Honest bidding is a naive rule that leaves money on the table.
Honest bidding is best in every auction format, whatever the other rules or information.
purposeDetail.ahaMoment: You drag your bid anywhere you like in the second-price auction, and the price you pay never moves until the exact point where you stop winning. The profit curve is flat across winning bids and drops off a cliff either side of your value, whereas the first-price curve has a hump below your value.
demos: Rung 1: a rising-price ladder auction with four simulated rivals; you choose when to drop out; the page replays the round with other dropout points.

Rung 2: sealed first-price round; type or drag a bid; the winner pays their own bid; a few single rounds, then a 5000-round replay shows average profit against bid as a fraction of value, peaking at the shaded point (n-1)/n.
Rung 3: sealed second-price round with the same slider; the profit curve now peaks exactly at honest bidding, and the page marks the winning-and-paying breakdown for any bid you choose.
Rung 4: what-if panel: change the number of rivals and watch the first-price best shade move toward honesty while second-price stays at honest.

Rung 5: break the guarantee: switch to a rule where the price follows your bid (first-price), or add a seller who can place a fake bid just under yours, or give bidders values that depend on each other; honest bidding stops being best, shown by arithmetic from the stated rules.
Rung 6: real world card: an advertising exchange moved from second-price to first-price auctions in 2019 and buyers added bid shading software; the rules changed the behaviour.
checkQuestions: Your value is 60 and the highest rival bids 45. You bid 50 in a second-price auction. What do you pay? (45)
Same values, first-price auction, bid 50. What is your profit? (10)
With 4 bidders with values spread evenly from 0 to 1, what share of your value should you bid in a first-price auction? (three quarters)
Name one change to the rules that stops honest bidding being best in a second-price auction.

research.summary: University course notes agree that truthful bidding is a dominant strategy in the second-price sealed-bid auction and that bidding (n-1)/n of value is the symmetric equilibrium of the first-price auction for uniform independent values. Lab studies repeatedly find real people overbid in the sealed second-price format yet learn the dominant strategy almost at once in the equivalent rising-price format, which justifies leading with the ladder. Ausubel and Milgrom's paper explains that the format is rare in practice despite its theoretical appeal, and Google's move to first-price auctions in 2019 gives a live example of rules reshaping behaviour. The brief's claim that honest bidding is best only when bids are sealed and simultaneous is imprecise: the equivalent rising-price auction gives the same strategy under private values, and what breaks it is first-price pricing or interdependent values.
